utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I hear as far as why the names were 12 excised, listening to Mr. Prpos, was he said those were not 13 relevant. The question becomes, well, who made the decision as 14 to relevancy? That is the problem. When they are turned over 15 to you and a decision is made by a person in power that, "This 16 is all I am going to give you", then that raises a problem just 17 in terms of our ability even to compel this individual to turn 18 over more. Certainly I imagine in any system, or at least in 19 any common law system, in terms of the completeness of a 20 document that is something that is recognised. What that means 21 is that one side should not be able to choose what it wants from 22 a document and put the document in and then not let the other 23 side see the entire document. I think that is a pretty 24 universal concept that would be recognised. Is that not true, 25 my fellow Judges? So the notion of completeness is not foreign and the 27 rationale is simple. It is to be fair for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have not made the decision on relevance. We have not told them to edit these documents. We were unable to see them until they were provided to us in this form. We have not asked for incomplete records to be put in this form before the Court. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Let me confer with my fellow Judges and see if they agree with me on my notion of completeness. Then of course there is a problem with just the production, whether we have the power even to do that. But there are questions I had about some of these documents and some names that I would be interested in. So it is going to affect how I might even look at these documents. (The Judges conferred). 12 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: My fellow Judges agree with my view on the notion of completeness, that is that if you offer part of a document then the other party can compel the entire document to be offered. The reason is obvious whether we are in common law or civil law I think. We want to have the complete document. The real power is our ability to compel. Judge Vohrah has suggested that there is no harm in asking the witness, directing him even, to produce the entire document. If he tells me, "Well, the powers that be made the decision that we would only give this", there is not too much I can tell him, I think, in terms of the power that this Tribunal has, unlike a national system. 24 MR. KAY: Yes, the Defence have no difficulty with the request. It is just that I am making a point to the Court about this as I do not want it reflected upon the Defence. 27 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I understand. I hope that the witness is still there and I will ask that he return. Do you have anything else to add, Miss Hollis, at this point? 2 MISS HOLLIS: Your Honour, we understood they were given these in redacted form. That is why we ask you to make the request, the order of this witness. We would note, however, that we have been told that in fact at least one or more of the Defence team have seen the unredacted documents even though they could not copy them. But again that really is peripheral I think to the problem here. 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: OK. Have you seen the complete document? 10 MR. KAY: Yes, but I cannot say I have memorized it or anything like that. 12 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It is Serbo-Croat and English. 13 MR. KAY: I insisted on seeing it so I knew what was being put before my eyes. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: The reasons that were given you for the redaction were? 17 MR. KAY: It is a need-to-know basis as far as I am concerned. 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Pardon me? 19 MR. KAY: I was being treated on a need-to-know basis. I was being given only what I was going to receive. 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: So did you ask for more and get only what you received? 23 MR. KAY: Yes, and I asked to make sure that I could see an authentic -- well, I will not give evidence, but I asked to see something so I knew where it came from. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I think it is appropriate since there was mention of the fact that a member of the Defence team had seen it. I do not think you are giving evidence out of sorts. Let us talk with Mr. Prpos. Mr. Marro, would you ask Mr. Prpos to put his earphones on, please. Mr. Prpos, this is Judge McDonald talking. Mr. Prpos, regarding certain Exhibits that you made reference to in your testimony, the Tribunal is requesting that you produce the complete copies of these Exhibits. The copies that we have been presented are only partial, in that certain names and other information is taken -- can you hear me still? Can you hear me? 9 THE WITNESS: I can hear you. I can hear you. I can hear you. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Certain information is taken out of these Exhibits. You referred to them when you said that information had been blanked out. The Tribunal is requesting that you produce these documents completely without the blanked out portions, and they are Exhibits 63 -- these are Defence Exhibits -- Defence Exhibit 63, 64, 65, 66, 75 and 77. Those are the documents that you made reference to today during your testimony. Are you able to produce those documents in their complete form without the blanked out portions or with the blanked out portions not being blanked out? 20 THE WITNESS: As far as I am concerned, because at present I am not in the Traffic Security police station, so all of that would be addressed to the present Commander of that station. So I do not have the authority now to give anything from those records because I am not authorised in that station now. These records remain in the station regardless of who is the Commander. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Who is the Commander again of the traffic police now? 28 THE WITNESS: At present it is Mile Jankovic. I have testified on the basis of what I know in relation to the documents that were made while I was Commander of the police station. 3 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Miss Hollis, is there anything else? Mr. Kay? Mile Jankovic I understand is the present Commander. 5 MISS HOLLIS: Yes, your Honour. 6 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: He is the person who would have custody of these records? 8 MISS HOLLIS: Yes, your Honour. 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I do not know how I could compel -- I was looking at the witness list and I do not see him as a witness for the Defence. 12 MR. KAY: He is not, your Honour. He declined. 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: So he is not a witness. What authority do I have to compel? 15 MISS HOLLIS: What actual authority you have to compel even with this witness I guess is a question, but I might suggest that you request of this witness to pass your request on to Mr. Jankovic and have a reply tomorrow. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: OK. Mr. Prpos, would you ask Mr. Jankovic if he will produce these documents in their complete form, the ones I referred to by Defence Exhibit numbers, so that you may bring them with you when you return tomorrow to complete your testimony? 24 THE WITNESS: I can try, but I cannot guarantee because this is exclusively within his authority. But I believe that insight can be made in a different way in terms of authenticating these documents. I think the people who have been crossed out are not all that important. These are simply the names of other policemen who do not want to appear in this kind of case. There are numbers and it is obvious that this is an excerpt in which Dusko Tadic appears. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: This is a trial and both sides want access to the information. So, if you will pass on this request, please, to Mr. Jankovic, and the request is that he give to you the complete copies of those Exhibits that I referred to by number, that is Defence Exhibits 63, 64, 65, 66, 75 and 77, so that you may bring them with you tomorrow. You indicate to him that that is a request that has been made by the Tribunal. Would you do that? 12 THE WITNESS: I shall tell him, but as far as the outcome is concerned I cannot be the judge of that. 14 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Thank you very much, Mr. Prpos. You are now excused until tomorrow at 10 a.m. and we will resume the testimony then. The Court is adjourned until 10 a.m. 17 THE WITNESS: Thank you. 18 (5.40 p.m.) (The court adjourned until the following day). 20 21 22 23 24 25 26 27 28
